opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the hesitation came from a few places at once.

The first was very personal. I had spent most of my life thinking of myself as a mathematician, someone who would do a PhD, prove theorems, and maybe stay in academia. Leaving that path felt like giving up an identity, not just a career plan. In math there's a romantic idea of the lone researcher sitting with a hard problem for years, and starting a company is almost the opposite of that. It's fast, it's collaborative, and it's full of things that have nothing to do with mathematics: hiring, fundraising, compute, operations.

The second was about timing and whether the problem was really ready. AI for math has had waves of excitement before, and many people in the community were skeptical, with good reason. I kept asking myself: is this real, or am I getting swept up in hype? Do language models actually reason, or are they pattern-matching in a way that will hit a wall? I didn't want to build a company on a premise that would collapse in two years.

The third was simply self-doubt. Many of the people working on this are at big labs with enormous resources. Who am I, a young person without a long track record of running things, to think a small team can compete in that environment?

What eventually changed my mind was seeing that the pieces were finally converging. Formal verification languages like Lean had matured, models were getting meaningfully better at reasoning, and there was a real gap between what the math community needed and what the general labs were focused on. I realized that if I waited until I felt fully ready, the window would pass. The hesitation never completely went away. I just decided the opportunity mattered more than the fear.

r001.rationale: The candidate mentions fundraising and the fast pace of startups, but does not identify a concern that long-term ambitions for AI in mathematics might conflict with the venture-capital cycle.

r002.rationale: The candidate separately expresses uncertainty about whether AI for math was real or hype, and self-doubt about whether she could build a company and compete with large labs.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the hesitation came from a few different places, and some of them were pretty personal.

The first was that I loved mathematics as a mathematician, not as a product. When you spend years in that world, you absorb this almost sacred idea that math is something you do slowly, for its own sake, in a room by yourself or with one collaborator at a blackboard. The idea of turning that into a company, with investors, deadlines, and a pitch deck, felt a little like betraying the thing I cared about. I worried I would stop being someone who does math and become someone who talks about math.

The second was timing. When I started thinking seriously about this, the models were not good at mathematics. They could produce something that looked like a proof, and if you read it quickly it was convincing, but it would collapse under scrutiny. And mathematics is unforgiving in a way most domains are not. A ninety percent correct proof is not a proof. So I kept asking myself whether this was a real moment or whether I was just excited because the demos were impressive. I did not want to build a company on a hope that the technology would arrive on schedule.

The third thing was the community. Mathematicians are skeptical people, rightly so, and many of them are uneasy about AI. I did not want to be the person who showed up and said, your field is about to be automated. I actually do not believe that is the right framing. But I knew that as soon as there was a company with my name on it, I would be read that way regardless of what I actually said.

What changed my mind was partly that the technology genuinely moved, especially with formal verification. Once you can have a machine check that a proof is actually correct, the problem stops being "does this sound right" and becomes "is this right," and that is a problem I believe can be worked on honestly. And partly it was realizing that if people who love mathematics do not build these tools, then people who do not will. I would rather be in the room shaping it than standing outside worrying about it.

astra-6.text: I think the hesitation was really about whether something intellectually exciting could also become a sustainable business. AI for mathematics is a compelling research direction, but that doesn’t automatically tell you who your first customer is or what they need badly enough to pay for. And there’s uncertainty on the technical side, too: can you make something reliable enough that mathematicians actually want to use it? Those were the questions that made me hesitant.

Mathematics is an exciting area for AI, but making progress on a research problem and building something people actually find useful are different things. I worried about that gap: could we turn an ambitious technical vision into a product, while still giving the research the time and freedom it needed?
